cards.front: How do cyclosporine and tacrolimus suppress T cells?
cards.back: Cyclosporine binds **cyclophilin**; tacrolimus binds **FKBP12**. Each complex blocks **calcineurin**, so the transcription factor **NFAT** stays phosphorylated in the cytoplasm. The T cell cannot make **IL-2**, so it does not proliferate.
cards.back_pt: A ciclosporina liga-se à **ciclofilina**; o tacrolimo liga-se à **FKBP12**. Cada complexo bloqueia a **calcineurina**, e o fator de transcrição **NFAT** permanece fosforilado no citoplasma. O linfócito T não produz **IL-2** e, assim, não prolifera.

cards.front: What are the main adverse effects of calcineurin inhibitors, and which are specific to cyclosporine?
cards.back: Both: **nephrotoxicity** (afferent arteriole constriction), **hypertension**, hyperkalemia, tremor and other neurotoxic effects, and hyperglycemia (worse with tacrolimus). Cyclosporine only: **gingival hyperplasia** and **hirsutism**.
cards.back_pt: Ambos: **nefrotoxicidade** (constrição da arteríola aferente), **hipertensão**, hipercalemia, tremor e outros efeitos neurotóxicos, e hiperglicemia (pior com tacrolimo). Só a ciclosporina: **hiperplasia gengival** e **hirsutismo**.

cards.front: How do sirolimus and everolimus differ from calcineurin inhibitors in mechanism and toxicity?
cards.back: They bind FKBP12 but inhibit **mTOR**, so T cells cannot **respond** to IL-2 (arrest in G1). **Less nephrotoxic** than calcineurin inhibitors. Main problems: **hyperlipidemia**, **cytopenias** and **poor wound healing**. Also coat **drug-eluting stents**.
cards.back_pt: Ligam-se à FKBP12, mas inibem a **mTOR**, e o linfócito T não consegue **responder** à IL-2 (parada em G1). **Menos nefrotóxicos** que os inibidores da calcineurina. Principais problemas: **hiperlipidemia**, **citopenias** e **cicatrização deficiente**. Também revestem **stents farmacológicos**.

cards.front: What do basiliximab, belatacept and antithymocyte globulin target in transplant patients?
cards.back: **Basiliximab**: monoclonal antibody against **CD25** (IL-2 receptor alpha chain). **Belatacept**: CTLA-4-Ig fusion protein that binds **CD80/CD86 (B7)**, blocking CD28 costimulation. **Antithymocyte globulin**: polyclonal antibodies that **deplete T cells**.
cards.back_pt: **Basiliximabe**: anticorpo monoclonal contra o **CD25** (cadeia alfa do receptor de IL-2). **Belatacepte**: proteína de fusão CTLA-4-Ig que se liga ao **CD80/CD86 (B7)** e bloqueia a coestimulação por CD28. **Globulina antitimocitária**: anticorpos policlonais que **depletam linfócitos T**.

cards.front: What does eculizumab block, and which infection risk follows?
cards.back: It binds **C5**, so C5 cannot be split and the **membrane attack complex** (C5b-9) does not form. Used in **PNH** and **atypical HUS**. Risk: severe ***Neisseria meningitidis*** infection, so patients get **meningococcal vaccines** first.
cards.back_pt: Liga-se ao **C5**, que não é clivado, e o **complexo de ataque à membrana** (C5b-9) não se forma. Usado na **HPN** e na **SHU atípica**. Risco: infecção grave por ***Neisseria meningitidis***; por isso, o paciente recebe antes **vacinas meningocócicas**.

cards.front: Why do live attenuated vaccines give strong immunity, and who should not receive them?
cards.back: The weakened microbe **replicates** inside host cells, so antigen is shown on **MHC I** and **MHC II**: strong **CD8+ cellular** and antibody responses. Avoid in **pregnancy** and in **significant immunosuppression**, where the vaccine strain can cause disease.
cards.back_pt: O micro-organismo atenuado **se replica** dentro das células do hospedeiro, e o antígeno é apresentado em **MHC I** e **MHC II**: forte resposta **celular CD8+** e de anticorpos. Evitar na **gestação** e na **imunossupressão significativa**, em que a cepa vacinal pode causar doença.

cards.front: Why does a conjugate vaccine work in infants when a plain polysaccharide vaccine does not?
cards.back: Plain polysaccharide is a **T-independent** antigen: mostly IgM, little memory, and poor responses in children under about 2 years. Linking it to a **carrier protein** recruits **CD4+ T helper cells**, giving **class switching** to IgG and **memory B cells**.
cards.back_pt: O polissacarídeo isolado é um antígeno **T-independente**: sobretudo IgM, pouca memória e resposta fraca em crianças com menos de cerca de 2 anos. A ligação a uma **proteína carreadora** recruta **linfócitos T CD4+ auxiliares**, com **troca de classe** para IgG e **linfócitos B de memória**.

cards.front: How does passive immunization with immune globulin differ from vaccination?
cards.back: It gives **preformed antibodies**: protection is **immediate** but lasts only weeks to months, with **no memory**. Examples: tetanus, rabies and hepatitis B immune globulins after exposure, often given **together with the vaccine** at a different site.
cards.back_pt: Fornece **anticorpos pré-formados**: a proteção é **imediata**, mas dura apenas semanas a meses, **sem memória**. Exemplos: imunoglobulinas antitetânica, antirrábica e anti-hepatite B após exposição, muitas vezes aplicadas **junto com a vacina** em outro local.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man had a kidney transplant 18 months ago. He takes prednisone, mycophenolate and a third immunosuppressive drug. He reports swollen gums that bleed when he brushes his teeth, and more hair on his face and back. Blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg. His gums are enlarged and partly cover the teeth. Serum creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 1.7 mg/dL, and potassium is 5.4 mEq/L. A graft biopsy shows arteriolar hyalinosis and striped interstitial fibrosis, with no signs of rejection. Which drug is the most likely third drug?
choices: Tacrolimus
Sirolimus
Cyclosporine
Azathioprine
Basiliximab
questions.explanation: **Cyclosporine** blocks calcineurin and causes **nephrotoxicity**, hypertension and hyperkalemia; **gingival hyperplasia** and **hirsutism** point to it specifically. **Tacrolimus** is the tempting choice: it shares the kidney, blood pressure and potassium effects, but it does not cause gingival overgrowth or hirsutism (it can cause hair loss). Sirolimus is not a typical cause of this nephrotoxicity, azathioprine causes mainly cytopenias, and basiliximab is used only for induction.
questions.explanation_pt: A **ciclosporina** bloqueia a calcineurina e causa **nefrotoxicidade**, hipertensão e hipercalemia; a **hiperplasia gengival** e o **hirsutismo** apontam especificamente para ela. O **tacrolimo** é a alternativa tentadora: compartilha os efeitos renais, pressóricos e sobre o potássio, mas não causa hiperplasia gengival nem hirsutismo (pode causar queda de cabelo). O sirolimo não é causa típica dessa nefrotoxicidade, a azatioprina causa sobretudo citopenias, e o basiliximabe é usado apenas na indução.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. For 1 year she has received an intravenous humanized monoclonal antibody every 2 weeks, and her hemolysis is well controlled. She now has 8 hours of fever, headache and a stiff neck. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, and pulse is 126/min. There is a non-blanching purpuric rash on her legs. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative diplococci. Which action of her drug best explains this infection?
choices: Blocking cleavage of C5, so the membrane attack complex cannot form
Blocking C3 convertase, so C3b opsonization fails
Depleting CD20-positive B cells, so antibody production falls
Neutralizing TNF-α, so granulomas cannot be maintained
Blocking the IL-2 receptor on activated T cells
questions.explanation: The drug is **eculizumab**, an anti-**C5** antibody used in PNH. Without C5 cleavage the **membrane attack complex** (C5b-9) cannot form, and the MAC is the main defense against ***Neisseria***; this is why patients receive **meningococcal vaccines** before therapy. The tempting answer, loss of **C3b opsonization**, would raise the risk of many encapsulated bacteria, but eculizumab acts after C3, so opsonization is preserved.
questions.explanation_pt: O fármaco é o **eculizumabe**, anticorpo anti-**C5** usado na HPN. Sem a clivagem do C5, o **complexo de ataque à membrana** (C5b-9) não se forma, e o MAC é a principal defesa contra ***Neisseria***; por isso, os pacientes recebem **vacinas meningocócicas** antes do tratamento. A alternativa tentadora, perda da **opsonização por C3b**, aumentaria o risco de várias bactérias encapsuladas, mas o eculizumabe atua depois do C3, e a opsonização é preservada.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy with sickle cell disease comes for a routine visit. A blood smear shows sickled cells and many red cells with small round nuclear remnants (Howell-Jolly bodies). His physician explains that he is at high risk of sepsis from encapsulated bacteria. He receives a pneumococcal vaccine in which capsular polysaccharides are chemically linked to a protein. Which mechanism best explains why this vaccine protects an infant, while a plain polysaccharide vaccine does not?
choices: The polysaccharide cross-links B-cell receptors and activates B cells without T-cell help
The protein carrier is a live organism that replicates and gives long-lasting antigen exposure
The conjugate is presented on MHC class I and activates CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
Macrophages process the polysaccharide into peptides that are shown on MHC class II
Carrier-protein peptides on MHC class II recruit help from CD4+ T cells
questions.explanation: Functional **asplenia** in sickle cell disease leaves the child open to encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, *H. influenzae* type b). In a **conjugate vaccine**, B cells that bind the polysaccharide take in the whole conjugate and show **carrier-protein peptides** on **MHC II**; **CD4+ T cells** then drive **class switching** to IgG and **memory**. The tempting first choice describes the **T-independent** response to a plain polysaccharide, which infants make poorly and which gives little memory. Polysaccharides are not processed into peptides for MHC presentation.
questions.explanation_pt: A **asplenia** funcional da doença falciforme deixa a criança vulnerável a bactérias encapsuladas (pneumococo, meningococo, *H. influenzae* tipo b). Na **vacina conjugada**, o linfócito B que reconhece o polissacarídeo internaliza todo o conjugado e apresenta **peptídeos da proteína carreadora** em **MHC II**; os **linfócitos T CD4+** então promovem a **troca de classe** para IgG e a **memória**. A primeira alternativa, tentadora, descreve a resposta **T-independente** ao polissacarídeo isolado, que o lactente produz mal e que gera pouca memória. Polissacarídeos não são processados em peptídeos para apresentação em MHC.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman had a kidney transplant 3 years ago. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and low-dose prednisone, and her graft function is stable. She plans a trip to a rural area of South America where yellow fever is endemic, and she asks which vaccines she can receive before the trip. Which vaccine is contraindicated for her?
choices: Recombinant (adjuvanted subunit) zoster vaccine
Yellow fever vaccine
Inactivated influenza vaccine by injection
Tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine
Hepatitis A inactivated vaccine
questions.explanation: The **yellow fever vaccine** is a **live attenuated** virus. In a patient on chronic **immunosuppression**, the vaccine strain can replicate without control and cause serious disease, so live vaccines are contraindicated. The tempting answer is the **zoster** vaccine, because the older zoster vaccine was live; the **recombinant** vaccine contains only a viral glycoprotein with an adjuvant and is safe in transplant recipients. The inactivated, toxoid and subunit vaccines listed cannot replicate.
questions.explanation_pt: A **vacina contra febre amarela** contém vírus **vivo atenuado**. Em paciente sob **imunossupressão** crônica, a cepa vacinal pode se replicar sem controle e causar doença grave; por isso, vacinas vivas são contraindicadas. A alternativa tentadora é a vacina contra **herpes-zóster**, porque a vacina antiga era de vírus vivo; a vacina **recombinante** contém apenas uma glicoproteína viral com adjuvante e é segura em transplantados. As vacinas inativadas, de toxoide e de subunidade listadas não se replicam.

notes.title: Immunosuppressants, immune-targeted biologics and vaccines
notes.body_md:
## Transplant immunosuppressants

- **Calcineurin inhibitors** (cyclosporine, tacrolimus): no **IL-2** transcription. **Nephrotoxicity**, hypertension, hyperkalemia, tremor, hyperglycemia. Cyclosporine adds **gingival hyperplasia** and **hirsutism**.
- **mTOR inhibitors** (sirolimus, everolimus): block the T-cell **response** to IL-2. Hyperlipidemia, cytopenias, poor wound healing; less nephrotoxic than calcineurin inhibitors.
- **Mycophenolate**: inhibits **IMP dehydrogenase**, so lymphocytes run short of guanine. GI upset, cytopenias; teratogenic. **Azathioprine**: see GI pharmacology.
- **Glucocorticoids**: broad suppression through less cytokine gene transcription.
- **Antibodies**: **basiliximab** (anti-CD25), **belatacept** (blocks B7-CD28 costimulation), **antithymocyte globulin** (T-cell depletion).

## Other immune-targeted drugs

- **Eculizumab**: anti-**C5**; no membrane attack complex, so **meningococcal** risk.
- **Omalizumab** (anti-IgE), anti-**IL-5** agents and **dupilumab** (IL-4 receptor alpha): see respiratory pharmacology.
- **Checkpoint inhibitors** (PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4): see hematology-oncology pharmacology.
- **Cytokines as drugs**: **interferon-α** (chronic hepatitis B, some cancers; flu-like illness, depression), **interferon-β** (multiple sclerosis), **interferon-γ** (chronic granulomatous disease), **aldesleukin** (IL-2; renal cell carcinoma and melanoma; **capillary leak**).

## Passive immunization

- Preformed antibodies: fast, short, no memory.
- Specific immune globulins (tetanus, rabies, hepatitis B) after exposure.
- **IVIG**: antibody deficiency, Kawasaki disease, immune thrombocytopenia. Anaphylaxis risk in **IgA deficiency** with anti-IgA antibodies.

## Vaccine types

- **Live attenuated**: replicate; strong cellular and antibody response. Avoid in **pregnancy** and **immunosuppression**.
- **Inactivated**: killed organism; mainly antibodies.
- **Subunit/recombinant**: purified antigen only; cannot replicate.
- **Conjugate**: a protein carrier makes polysaccharide **T-dependent**, so infants respond.
- **Toxoid** (tetanus, diphtheria): antibodies against the toxin, not the bacterium.
- **mRNA** and **viral vector**: host cells make the antigen; mRNA does not enter the nucleus.
- **Asplenia**: vaccinate against **pneumococcus**, **meningococcus** and **Hib**.

## Adverse effects to know

- **Rotavirus** vaccine: small risk of **intussusception**.
- **Guillain-Barré syndrome**: rare link with some vaccines, classically influenza.
notes.body_pt_md:
## Imunossupressores no transplante

- **Inibidores da calcineurina** (ciclosporina, tacrolimo): sem transcrição de **IL-2**. **Nefrotoxicidade**, hipertensão, hipercalemia, tremor, hiperglicemia. A ciclosporina causa também **hiperplasia gengival** e **hirsutismo**.
- **Inibidores da mTOR** (sirolimo, everolimo): bloqueiam a **resposta** do linfócito T à IL-2. Hiperlipidemia, citopenias, cicatrização deficiente; menos nefrotóxicos que os inibidores da calcineurina.
- **Micofenolato**: inibe a **IMP desidrogenase**, e os linfócitos ficam sem guanina. Sintomas gastrointestinais, citopenias; teratogênico. **Azatioprina**: ver farmacologia gastrointestinal.
- **Glicocorticoides**: supressão ampla por menor transcrição de genes de citocinas.
- **Anticorpos**: **basiliximabe** (anti-CD25), **belatacepte** (bloqueia a coestimulação B7-CD28), **globulina antitimocitária** (depleção de linfócitos T).

## Outros fármacos dirigidos ao sistema imune

- **Eculizumabe**: anti-**C5**; sem complexo de ataque à membrana, daí o risco **meningocócico**.
- **Omalizumabe** (anti-IgE), agentes anti-**IL-5** e **dupilumabe** (receptor alfa da IL-4): ver farmacologia respiratória.
- **Inibidores de checkpoint** (PD-1, PD-L1, CTLA-4): ver farmacologia hematológica e oncológica.
- **Citocinas como fármacos**: **alfainterferona** (hepatite B crônica, alguns cânceres; quadro gripal, depressão), **betainterferona** (esclerose múltipla), **gamainterferona** (doença granulomatosa crônica), **aldesleucina** (IL-2; carcinoma de células renais e melanoma; **extravasamento capilar**).

## Imunização passiva

- Anticorpos pré-formados: rápida, curta, sem memória.
- Imunoglobulinas específicas (antitetânica, antirrábica, anti-hepatite B) após exposição.
- **IGIV** (em inglês, IVIG): deficiência de anticorpos, doença de Kawasaki, trombocitopenia imune. Risco de anafilaxia na **deficiência de IgA** com anticorpos anti-IgA.

## Tipos de vacina

- **Viva atenuada**: replica-se; forte resposta celular e de anticorpos. Evitar na **gestação** e na **imunossupressão**.
- **Inativada**: micro-organismo morto; sobretudo anticorpos.
- **Subunidade/recombinante**: apenas o antígeno purificado; não se replica.
- **Conjugada**: a proteína carreadora torna o polissacarídeo **T-dependente**, e o lactente responde.
- **Toxoide** (tétano, difteria): anticorpos contra a toxina, não contra a bactéria.
- **mRNA** e **vetor viral**: as células do hospedeiro produzem o antígeno; o mRNA não entra no núcleo.
- **Asplenia**: vacinar contra **pneumococo**, **meningococo** e **Hib**.

## Efeitos adversos a conhecer

- Vacina contra **rotavírus**: pequeno risco de **intussuscepção** (invaginação intestinal).
- **Síndrome de Guillain-Barré**: associação rara com algumas vacinas, classicamente a da influenza.
